sources.citation: Petitot, Emile. 1891. Autour du Grand Lac des Esclaves. Paris: A. Savine. (CIHM 11181, archive.org scanned text)
sources.note: Nothing; the four 'jargon' hits all concern the Mackenzie 'jargon esclave' (Broken Slavey, brok1250), e.g. 'Etin! douye. Seni (Vois plus rien), dit-il dans le jargon esclave qu'ont invente les creoles du Mackenzie'. No mention of the Loucheux/Youkon jargon.

sources.citation: Petitot, Emile. 1889. Quinze ans sous le Cercle Polaire: Mackenzie, Anderson, Youkon. Paris: E. Dentu. (CIHM 15868, archive.org scanned text; Fort Youkon chapter pp. ca. 284-294)
sources.note: Nothing. The only primary attestation of the jargon: two quoted utterances of the 'jargon du Youkon' with French glosses (e.g. 'Allons, nos gens, dji dindjie jette a l'eau, apres ca tikke anl'a nipaa walili. Esdiniye djan api, esdiniye djan nene kke bepaenda') and the footnote 'Le jargon loucheux, qui a cours dans le Youkon comme chez les Dindjie de Peel-River, se compose de lambeaux de francais, d'anglais, de tchippewayan, d'esclave, de dindjie et meme de cris. Il n'a pas cours dans le Mackenzie, ou regne le jargon esclave.' No remark on pronunciation, accent or stress.

sources.citation: Dall, William H. 1870. Alaska and its resources. Boston: Lee and Shepard. (archive.org alaskaitsresourc00dallrich, scanned text)
sources.note: Nothing. Contemporary (1867) note on the Fort Yukon contact language only: 'the usual mode of communication between the whites and Indians in this locality is a jargon somewhat like Chinook, known by the name of "Broken Slave." The basis of this jargon, which includes many modified French and English words, is the dialect of Liard River.' (the scanned textprinted p. ~106); also 'Husky.. is also found in the Broken Slave jargon with the same meaning' (glossary). No linguistic description, no stress.
Nothing on phonology; used only for its reference list (McClellan 1981, Bakker 1996, Slobodin 1981, Petitot 1889, Dall 1870, Krauss 1983, Mishler 2008, Campbell 1997).

sources.citation: Bakker, Peter. 1996. Broken Slavey and Jargon Loucheux: a first exploration. In Broch & Jahr (eds.), Language Contact in the Arctic: Northern Pidgins and Contact Languages, 317-320. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

sources.note: The only linguistic treatment named specifically for Jargon Loucheux; 4 pages, would confirm whether any phonological/prosodic remark exists (almost certainly not, given the data base is Petitot's few sentences).

sources.citation: Mishler, Craig. 2008. 'That's a Rubbaboo': Slavey Jargon in a nineteenth century Subarctic speech community. Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 23(2): 264-287.

sources.note: Fullest modern study of the Gwich'in-area jargon (Fort McPherson / La Pierre's House / Fort Yukon = Jargon Loucheux territory) with texts from fluent Gwich'in speakers; the one place a remark on how jargon words were pronounced/accented could appear. Abstract mentions only lexicon, grammar and sociolinguistics.
